Title: Chapter 13 -multi-scale modeling of tissues using compucell3d
Abstract: The study of how cells interact to produce tissue development, homeostasis, or diseases was, until recently, almost purely experimental. Now, multi-cell computer simulation methods, ranging from relatively simple cellular automata to complex immersed-boundary and finite-element mechanistic models, allow in silico study of multi-cell phenomena at the tissue scale based on biologically observed cell behaviors and interactions such as movement, adhesion, growth, death, mitosis, secretion of chemicals, chemotaxis, etc. This tutorial introduces the lattice-based Glazier–Graner–Hogeweg (GGH) Monte Carlo multi-cell modeling and the open-source GGH-based CompuCell3D simulation environment that allows rapid and intuitive modeling and simulation of cellular and multi-cellular behaviors in the context of tissue formation and subsequent dynamics. We also present a walkthrough of four biological models and their associated simulations that demonstrate the capabilities of the GGH and CompuCell3D.

gold.abstract: Mechanistic, multicellular, agent-based models are commonly used to investigate tissue, organ, and organism-scale biology at single-cell resolution. The Cellular-Potts Model (CPM) is a powerful and popular framework for developing and interrogating these models. CPMs become computationally expensive at large space- and time- scales making application and investigation of developed models difficult. Surrogate models may allow for the accelerated evaluation of CPMs of complex biological systems. However, the stochastic nature of these models means each set of parameters may give rise to different model configurations, complicating surrogate model development. In this work, we leverage denoising diffusion probabilistic models to train a generative AI surrogate of a CPM used to investigate in vitro vasculogenesis. We describe the use of an image classifier to learn the characteristics that define unique areas of a 2-dimensional parameter space. We then apply this classifier to aid in surrogate model selection and verification. Our CPM model surrogate generates model configurations 20,000 timesteps ahead of a reference configuration and demonstrates approximately a 22x reduction in computational time as compared to native code execution. Our work represents a step towards the implementation of DDPMs to develop digital twins of stochastic biological systems.
gold.explanation: AI surrogate of a CPM used to investigate in vitro vasculogenesis. We describe the use of an image classifier to learn the characteristics that define unique areas of a 2-dimensional parameter space. We then apply this classifier to aid in surrogate model selection and verification.
gold.title: Generative diffusion model surrogates for mechanistic agent-based biological models

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:

CompuCell3D tissue configurations supply domain geometry and boundary conditions (cell clusters as flow/thermal obstacles, secretion sources/sinks). Paper-c’s cGAN maps these configurations to steady temperature/flow fields. The fields return to CompuCell3D as extracellular cues—e.g., chemotaxis up a gradient, or proliferation/death based on local heat—coupling GGH cell dynamics to transport without solving PDEs inside the loop.

Measure cGAN MAE against finite-difference/CFD solutions for temperature and velocity on held-out geometries. Then run hybrid GGH-cGAN simulations with transport-dependent cell rules; compare tissue metrics (cluster size, interface length, cell density, front speed) against a full PDE-GGH benchmark. Validate agreement and record computational speedup across parameter sweeps of adhesion and source strength.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose coupling CompuCell3D’s GGH tissue model to paper-c’s cGAN transport solver: tissue geometry and boundary conditions drive cGAN inference of steady heat/flow fields, which feed back as chemotactic, death, or proliferation cues. This tests whether a learned transport surrogate preserves tissue-scale emergent dynamics while reducing computational cost relative to full PDE coupling.

FINAL IDEA: Use paper-c’s cGAN transport solver as the extracellular field engine inside CompuCell3D’s GGH tissue simulations, linking cellular adhesion, growth, secretion, and chemotaxis to predicted heat and flow fields for accelerated multi-scale modeling.

--- Researcher C ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
I adopt Paper B (from Researcher A): CompuCell3D GGH multi-cell modeling of adhesion, growth, death, mitosis, secretion, and chemotaxis for tissue-scale dynamics. I adopt Paper-c (from Researcher B): a conditional GAN that maps arbitrary boundary conditions and domain geometry to steady-state heat/flow fields, validated by MAE and fast inference. I reject both colleagues’ conclusion that no second source exists; taken together, they provide the two required contributions.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Use the conditional GAN as a learned steady-state transport surrogate inside CompuCell3D. Instead of solving extracellular reaction-diffusion PDEs at each step, CompuCell3D passes the current cell-geometry mask and boundary/source-sink conditions to the GAN; the GAN returns oxygen/flow fields; cells then read these fields for metabolism, chemotaxis, and death. This creates a two-way feedback: cell dynamics alter geometry, geometry alters predicted transport, transport alters cells.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Train the GAN on paired data generated by CompuCell3D’s full PDE oxygen solver across varied cell masks, domain shapes, and oxygen boundary values. In hybrid runs, every 50 Monte Carlo steps compute the mask, query the GAN, and apply resulting oxygen to cell rules. Compare hybrid vs. full-solver CompuCell3D over 7-day in silico spheroid growth: oxygen-field MAE, necrotic-core radius, viable-cell count, and wall-clock speedup. Validate with 5-fold cross-validation and equivalence margins. Qualification: limited to steady-state transport; transient coupling remains untested.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
We propose coupling CompuCell3D multicellular tissue dynamics with a conditional GAN surrogate for steady-state transport. Cell configurations generate geometry and boundary conditions for the GAN, which rapidly predicts oxygen/flow fields that feed back into cell movement, growth, and death. We train on CompuCell3D PDE outputs and validate accuracy and speedup against full-solver simulations of tumor spheroid growth. This provides fast, scalable multiscale feedback unavailable in either source alone.

FINAL IDEA: Integrate a conditional GAN transport surrogate into CompuCell3D’s cell-dynamics loop so tissue geometry and predicted oxygen/flow fields co-evolve rapidly, enabling large-scale multiscale simulations.
